title: A Vortex Avalanche Model for Pulsar Glitches
abstract: Pulsar glitches are thought to involve sudden unpinning and fast transport of large numbers of pinned vortices, possibly triggered by breaking of the neutron star crust solid. Such a vortex avalanche can take place on a fast timescale only if there are pathways for fast vortex motion. Formation of local vortex ``traps'' (regions containing larger than average density of pinned vortices) will provide vortex-free regions surrounding the traps, which can connect to form pathways for fast vortex motion. We propose a simple two-dimensional model for the neutron star crust superfluid, with the vortex pinning landscape tiled into traps and surrounding vortex-free regions which can connect to azimuthal pathways for fast vortex motion. The trap and tile sizes are estimated from the physics of the crust solid and vortex pinning, namely the critical strain angle of the crust solid and the critical velocity for vortex unpinning. Unpinned vortices move with the superfluid flow in the azimuthal direction while also scattering radially outward, by a small angle, due to mutual friction. The model qualitatively explains the glitch parameters and their evolution in young pulsars and provides an explanation for the bi-modality in the distribution of glitch magnitudes. Laboratory experiments and simulations on vortex systems with spatially inhomogeneous vortex pinning landscapes are likely to be more realistic models for pulsar glitches. Breaking the spatial scale-invariance and monitoring the results may also lead to better understanding of collective behaviour in pinned vortex systems in general.
summary: This paper introduces a Vortex Avalanche Model to explain pulsar glitches, treating the neutron star superfluid as a lattice of pinned vortex traps. The model simulates the sudden release of angular momentum when these vortices unpin rapidly, successfully explaining key observational features like the bimodal distribution of glitch sizes. It emphasizes that the geometry of the pinning landscape is crucial for the avalanche dynamics.
main_problem: The paper models pulsar glitches, sudden spin-up events in pulsars, by proposing a mechanism involving the rapid unpinning and transport of quantized vortices within the neutron star's superfluid.
main_result: The proposed vortex avalanche model qualitatively explains observed glitch parameters, including the bi-modality in the distribution of glitch magnitudes, by requiring the breaking of spatial scale-invariance.
method: The authors developed a two-dimensional model treating the vortex pinning landscape as a tiling of 'traps' and 'vortex-free regions' to simulate the avalanche dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is the superfluid component of a neutron star, where quantized vortices interact with the solid crust. The model treats the pinning landscape as a periodic structure of traps and pathways, governing vortex motion via mutual friction and pinning forces.
key_observables: Pulsar glitch parameters ($\Delta\Omega/\Omega$), the distribution of glitch magnitudes (observed to be bimodal), and the evolution of glitch size with pulsar age.
important_parameters: Critical strain angle of the crust solid, critical velocity for vortex unpinning ($v_{cr}$), trap size ($D$), and tile size ($D'$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes that the glitch is caused by a vortex avalanche propagating through pathways connecting localized vortex traps, and that the physics is governed by the geometry of the pinning landscape.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the crust superfluid as a strip tiled by vortex traps (squares of side D) within larger domains (D'), visualizing the geometry of the model.
paper_structure: The paper builds from the general problem of pulsar glitches to proposing a 2D model of the superfluid. It details the physics of vortex motion (creep, pinning forces), develops the avalanche mechanism based on trap geometry, and finally relates the resulting glitch size to observable parameters like the moment of inertia ratio ($ eta$).
why_interesting: While focused on astrophysics, the underlying physics—collective dynamics in a highly constrained, disordered, and inhomogeneous medium (pinned vortices)—shares conceptual links with models of glassy dynamics or charge transport in disordered solids.
